servicesMeta.headline: Engineering help, scoped to the problem
servicesMeta.intro: Every engagement starts the same way. Find the real constraint, design against it, build it properly, then prove the result with numbers. Below is the work I take on, led by the e-commerce specialisation that has taken up most of the last five years.

services.title: E-Commerce Engineering
services.shortDescription: Salesforce Commerce Cloud storefronts and the APIs behind them, from product discovery through payment settlement.
services.problem: Commerce platforms fail quietly. Cart abandonment creeps up, checkout errors get absorbed as support tickets, and nobody can point to the line of code responsible.
services.solution: I work inside SFCC the way it is actually built, across SFRA controllers, cartridges, jobs and the OCAPI/SCAPI surface, and treat the discovery-to-payment journey as one system rather than a set of pages.
problemsSolved: Cart and checkout flows that lose users at a step nobody has instrumented.
Product listing and detail pages that degrade as catalogue size grows.
Payment and fraud integrations that fail in ways the storefront cannot recover from.
Fulfilment complexity such as multi-shipment, in-store pickup and same-day delivery.
Order export, OMS handoff and settlement jobs that break silently overnight.

engineeringApproach.title: Map the journey against real data
engineeringApproach.description: Before changing anything, I trace the discovery-to-cart path and find where users and requests actually drop. The redesign follows the data, not an opinion about layout.

engineeringApproach.title: Design the contract first
engineeringApproach.description: Storefront and middleware get a versioned API contract up front, so the mobile app, web front end and partner integrations can move independently.

engineeringApproach.title: Build on platform grain
engineeringApproach.description: Cartridges, hooks and jobs are written the way SFCC expects, which keeps upgrades cheap and keeps custom code out of the platform's way.

engineeringApproach.title: Prove the change
engineeringApproach.description: Conversion, abandonment and latency are measured before and after. Work that cannot be measured does not get called a success.

architectureConsiderations: Headless and hybrid storefronts have different failure modes. The choice gets made against the client's roadmap, not fashion.
OCAPI and SCAPI overlap but are not interchangeable. Picking the wrong one costs a migration later.
Checkout must degrade safely when a payment or fraud provider is slow or down.
Catalogue and inventory feeds define the real performance ceiling for discovery pages.

proofMetric.label: lower cart abandonment after a PLP/PDP redesign

services.title: Backend Engineering
services.shortDescription: Java and Spring Boot services, Node.js middleware, and REST or GraphQL APIs designed to be built against.
services.problem: Backends get built endpoint by endpoint until the data model no longer matches the domain, and every new feature needs a workaround.
services.solution: I model the domain first, set service boundaries deliberately, and build APIs with versioning, auth and failure behaviour decided before the first handler is written.
problemsSolved: APIs whose contracts change under their consumers.
Data models that fight the domain instead of describing it.
Authentication and role-based access bolted on after launch.
Services with no test coverage on the paths that carry money.
Slow endpoints where nobody has separated database time from application time.

engineeringApproach.title: Model the domain before the endpoints
engineeringApproach.description: Entities, relationships and invariants get written down first. The API then exposes that model rather than inventing a second one.

engineeringApproach.title: Decide the contract and its versioning
engineeringApproach.description: Request and response shapes, error semantics and deprecation policy are part of the design, not something discovered in integration testing.

engineeringApproach.title: Make failure explicit
engineeringApproach.description: Timeouts, retries, idempotency and circuit breaking are designed in. A dependency being down should be a handled case, not an outage.

engineeringApproach.title: Test the paths that matter
engineeringApproach.description: Unit tests for logic and integration tests for the flows that touch persistence, payments or external partners.

architectureConsiderations: Relational or document storage is chosen against the access pattern, not by preference.
Service boundaries follow the domain. Splitting too early costs more than a well-structured monolith.
Caching needs an invalidation story before it gets added, otherwise it trades correctness for speed.
Auth and RBAC belong in the design phase because retrofitting them touches every endpoint.

services.title: System Architecture
services.shortDescription: High and low level design, service boundaries, data modelling and the trade-off decisions that are expensive to reverse.
services.problem: The costly decisions get made early, often implicitly, and by the time the cost shows up the system has been built on top of them.
services.solution: I produce the design work that makes those decisions explicit: capacity estimates, boundaries, data flow, consistency trade-offs and a migration path that a team can actually execute.
problemsSolved: Monoliths that need splitting without a plan for the data.
Platform migrations where the cutover risk has never been written down.
Systems that work at current load with no estimate of where they break.
Teams disagreeing about service ownership because boundaries were never defined.
Consistency requirements that were assumed rather than agreed.

engineeringApproach.title: Requirements and capacity first
engineeringApproach.description: Traffic shape, growth, read and write ratios and latency budgets get estimated before any diagram is drawn.

engineeringApproach.title: Model the domain, then cut the boundaries
engineeringApproach.description: Services are separated along domain seams where data ownership is clean, rather than along team structure or convenience.

engineeringApproach.title: Name the trade-offs out loud
engineeringApproach.description: Consistency against availability, sharding strategy, cache invalidation and coupling all get stated with their cost, so the decision is the client's to make.

engineeringApproach.title: Write an executable migration path
engineeringApproach.description: A design that cannot be shipped incrementally is not finished. Each phase gets a rollback story.

architectureConsiderations: Consistent hashing and sharding decisions are effectively permanent once data volume grows.
Every network hop added between services is a new failure mode and a new latency budget.
Read-heavy and write-heavy paths usually want different storage strategies.
Incident response and observability are architecture, not operations afterthoughts.

services.title: Performance Engineering
services.shortDescription: Profiling, caching strategy and targeted optimisation on the paths that carry revenue.
services.problem: Performance work often starts with a hunch, changes ten things at once, and finishes with no evidence it helped.
services.solution: I establish a baseline, profile the real request path, fix what the profile points at, and verify against the same measurement.
problemsSolved: Checkout and cart latency that costs conversion at peak traffic.
Database queries that were fine at launch and are not fine now.
Memory pressure and garbage collection pauses in JVM services.
Thread contention and shared-state bugs that only appear under load.
Caching added without an invalidation strategy, producing stale data.

engineeringApproach.title: Establish a baseline worth comparing against
engineeringApproach.description: Real traffic, realistic data volume and percentile latency rather than averages. An average hides the users who leave.

engineeringApproach.title: Profile before changing anything
engineeringApproach.description: Application time, database time and network time get separated, so effort goes where the time actually is.

engineeringApproach.title: Change one thing at a time
engineeringApproach.description: Each optimisation is measured on its own. Bundled changes make it impossible to know what worked.

engineeringApproach.title: Leave monitoring behind
engineeringApproach.description: The work is not finished until regressions will be caught by instrumentation rather than by a customer.

architectureConsiderations: A cache is a correctness decision before it is a speed decision.
Async processing moves latency out of the user path but adds delivery guarantees to think about.
Percentile latency matters more than mean for anything user-facing.
Optimising a path that carries two percent of traffic is a waste of a sprint.
deliverables: Implemented fixes with before and after numbers

proofMetric.label: higher checkout conversion after backend redesign

services.title: API Development & Integrations
services.shortDescription: Payments, fraud, OMS, mobile middleware and partner APIs, integrated with failure behaviour designed in.
services.problem: Integrations are where systems break, because the other side has its own uptime, its own rate limits and its own idea of what an error means.
services.solution: I design integrations defensively, with explicit contracts, idempotency, retry policy and a defined behaviour for every way the partner can fail.
problemsSolved: Payment and fraud providers that time out mid-checkout.
Mobile apps needing a stable API layer over a commerce platform.
Order export and OMS handoff that fails without anyone noticing.
Duplicate charges or duplicate orders from naive retry logic.
Partner APIs with rate limits that the integration ignores.

engineeringApproach.title: Agree the contract with both sides
engineeringApproach.description: Payload shape, authentication, error codes and rate limits get documented before implementation, which removes most integration-phase surprises.

engineeringApproach.title: Make every write idempotent
engineeringApproach.description: Anything that creates an order or moves money is safe to retry. That single decision prevents an entire category of incident.

engineeringApproach.title: Move slow work off the user path
engineeringApproach.description: Fraud checks, exports and settlements run asynchronously so a slow partner does not become a slow checkout.

engineeringApproach.title: Instrument the seam
engineeringApproach.description: Every integration gets logging, alerting and a replay path, because the failures that matter happen at three in the morning.

architectureConsiderations: Synchronous calls to a partner put their uptime inside your uptime.
Retries without idempotency keys create duplicates rather than resilience.
Webhook receivers need to be idempotent and to verify signatures.
Versioning matters most where you do not control the consumer.

services.title: AI Engineering
services.shortDescription: Retrieval, structured outputs, function calling and the guardrails that make an LLM feature safe to ship.
services.problem: Most LLM features demo well and fail in production, because nothing was built to evaluate them, constrain them or defend them against hostile input.
services.solution: I treat an AI feature as a system with a contract. Structured outputs, retrieval that can be inspected, evaluations that catch regressions, and guardrails against prompt injection.
problemsSolved: Model output that cannot be parsed reliably by downstream code.
Retrieval that returns plausible but wrong context.
No way to tell whether a prompt change made quality better or worse.
Agent tooling with no boundary on what it is allowed to do.
User-supplied content being treated as instructions by the model.

engineeringApproach.title: Define the output contract
engineeringApproach.description: Structured outputs and schema validation first, so downstream code has something dependable to consume.

engineeringApproach.title: Make retrieval inspectable
engineeringApproach.description: Hybrid search over embeddings plus keyword matching, with the retrieved context logged so a bad answer can be traced to its source.

engineeringApproach.title: Build evals before tuning
engineeringApproach.description: A prompt change without an evaluation set is a guess. The eval suite comes first and runs on every change.

engineeringApproach.title: Treat external text as hostile
engineeringApproach.description: Content pulled from users, documents or the web is data, never instructions. Guardrails and injection defence are part of the design.

architectureConsiderations: Latency and cost per call shape the architecture as much as quality does.
Retrieval quality usually matters more than model choice.
Agent state and tool permissions need explicit boundaries.
Every model-facing feature needs a deterministic fallback.
